newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission approves animal disease programme.
newsitem.headline: Commission approves animal disease programme.

text.p: The European Commission said on Wednesday it had agreed to a plan by Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler to spend 67 million Ecus in 1997 eradicating animal diseases which threaten human health.

The budget includes 5.43 million Ecus to continue what a statement described as "...the very successful campaign against rabies, concentrating on the few remaining pockets of infected wildlife in the (European) Community ....".
The programme will include maintaining a 100 km (60-mile) 'vaccination barrier zone' along the European Union's eastern border.
An offical said the anti-rabies programme would soon make quarantine in Britain and Ireland irrelevant.
"The British and Irish rabies laws have been irrelevant in the view of the Commission for some time now. They will soon be an anachronism," a Commission official said.
The British government has said it is considering the future of the country's rabies quarantine laws.
The new budget for 1997 will also include 24.2 million Ecus to eradicate brucellosis in sheep and goats in southern EU countries. The disease can cause the often fatal Malta fever in humans.
Altogether 12 major diseases which have implications for human health or can cause livestock losses and barriers to trade are to be targeted.
Mad cow disease is not included. The BSE (bovine spongiform encephalopathy) crisis is financed separately under the EU's FEOGA agricultural guarantee fund.

The disease has cost the EU farm budget 2.0 billion Ecus this year. The figure includes 1.2 billion spent on beef intervention (market support) measures. The cull of thirty month old cows in Britain has cost 200 million this year and will cost a further 360 million in 1997, a Commission official said.
